techniques.name: Parboiling
techniques.mechanism: Hot water gelatinizes surface starch so the edges can later dehydrate and brown.
techniques.disagreement: Some recipes roast from raw; others insist on a boil so the surface can roughen.
techniques.skip_supported: Side-by-side roast-potato tests report a smoother surface and slower browning when potatoes go into the oven raw.
techniques.skip_predicted: The interior may stay firmer for longer; crust area is expected to decrease because less gelatinized starch is available to dry and brown.
techniques.default_step: Cover cut potatoes with cold salted water and simmer until the edges just yield to a knife.

techniques.name: Roughening the surface
techniques.mechanism: Agitating par-cooked potatoes shears hydrated starch into a thin paste that later dries into a crust.
techniques.disagreement: Some cooks only drain; others shake the pan until the potatoes look coated in mash.
techniques.skip_supported: Recipe tests that skip the shake step report fewer crags and a thinner crust than potatoes tossed until ragged.
techniques.skip_predicted: Browning still occurs on flat faces, but total crisp area should be smaller.
techniques.default_step: Drain the potatoes and shake the pot until the edges look coated in a thin starch paste.

techniques.name: Adding baking soda
techniques.mechanism: A mildly alkaline boil weakens pectin so the surface breaks down faster and more starch is freed for crust.
techniques.disagreement: Some recipes add baking soda to the water; others warn it can taste soapy or make the potatoes collapse.
techniques.skip_supported: Comparative recipes find baking soda speeds surface breakdown; many testers still get a crust from a plain salted boil if they roughen well.
techniques.skip_predicted: Without alkali, edges should need a longer simmer to reach the same ragged surface. A large dose is expected to taste alkaline.
techniques.default_step: Add about 1/2 teaspoon baking soda per 2 liters of water before the simmer.

techniques.name: High-temperature roasting
techniques.mechanism: Dry heat above roughly 200 C drives off surface water and promotes Maillard browning on the starch crust.
techniques.disagreement: Recipes split between a moderate oven for even cooking and a very hot oven or preheated pan for crust.
techniques.skip_supported: Lower-temperature roasts in published comparisons stay paler and take longer to dry.
techniques.skip_predicted: The interior can still cook through, but the crust should form more slowly and may stay leathery if moisture remains.
techniques.default_step: Roast on a preheated sheet at 220 C / 425 F, turning once, until the crust is deeply browned.

techniques.name: Drying before oiling
techniques.purpose: Removes surface water that blocks browning
techniques.mechanism: Water on the surface must evaporate before the temperature can rise into the Maillard range.
techniques.disagreement: Some recipes oil potatoes while wet; others steam-dry them in the pot or on a rack first.
techniques.skip_supported: Testers who oil wet potatoes report more steaming and paler sides until the water cooks off.
techniques.skip_predicted: Oil is expected to slide off a wet surface, and browning should start later.
techniques.default_step: Return the drained potatoes to the hot pot for a minute so surface moisture steams off, then toss with oil.

techniques.name: Salting meat ahead
techniques.purpose: Seasons below the surface and dries the exterior
techniques.mechanism: Salt first draws moisture, then dissolves and moves inward; the surface later dries, which helps browning.
techniques.disagreement: Some cooks salt just before the pan; others salt 40 minutes to a day ahead.
techniques.skip_supported: Steak tests show last-minute salting seasons the crust but not the interior; a mid-wait wet surface can slow browning.
techniques.skip_predicted: Flavor should stay closer to the surface. A short rest after salting may leave the exterior wetter than either immediate cooking or a long dry brine.
techniques.default_step: Salt the steak generously and rest it uncovered until the surface looks dry again, or cook immediately after salting.

techniques.name: Oil in pasta water
techniques.purpose: Claimed to stop noodles from sticking
techniques.mechanism: Oil floats and does not coat submerged starch; sticking is reduced by plenty of water and stirring, not by a film of fat.
techniques.disagreement: Home recipes often add oil to the pot; many restaurant cooks and testers say it does nothing useful and can keep sauce from clinging.
techniques.skip_supported: Controlled pasta tests find oil in the water does not stop pieces from welding, and leftover oil can make sauce slide off.
techniques.skip_predicted: Skipping the oil should not increase sticking if the pot is large and the pasta is stirred in the first minute.
techniques.default_step: Skip oil in the water. Use a wide pot, salt the water, and stir during the first minute of boiling.

techniques.name: Long fermentation
techniques.purpose: Develops flavor and a more extensible dough
techniques.mechanism: Yeast and enzymes slowly produce acids and break down flour proteins and starches during a cold or room-temperature rest.
techniques.disagreement: One pizza dough is mixed and baked the same day; another rests 24 hours or more.
techniques.skip_supported: Same-day doughs in side-by-side pizza tests are less tangy and can be tighter unless the flour is strong and the hydration is managed.
techniques.skip_predicted: A two-hour dough can still open and brown if gluten is developed, but flavor complexity and oven spring are expected to be lower.
techniques.default_step: Mix a wet dough, rest it cold for 24 hours, then temper before stretching.

techniques.name: Short fermentation
techniques.purpose: Gets a bakeable dough the same day
techniques.mechanism: A warmer, yeastier mix develops gas quickly with less acid and less enzymatic softening.
techniques.disagreement: Quick doughs trade flavor and extensibility for speed.
techniques.skip_supported: Published same-day pizza methods work when hydration and kneading compensate; they rarely match a 24-hour cold ferment in aroma.
techniques.skip_predicted: Skipping a short ferment in favor of a long one should increase acidity and relaxation if the yeast load is reduced.
techniques.default_step: If time is short, use slightly more yeast and a warmer rest, and expect milder flavor.

techniques.name: Egg replacement in baking
techniques.purpose: Stands in for binding, fat, or lift when eggs are omitted
techniques.mechanism: Eggs contribute protein structure, emulsified fat, and steam. Replacers copy one of those jobs, not all of them.
techniques.disagreement: One substitute is recommended for every bake; testers find flax binds cookies, aquafaba foams cakes, and fruit puree adds moisture more than structure.
techniques.skip_supported: Bake-off notes show a single replacer fails across cakes, cookies, and custards because those goods lean on different egg functions.
techniques.skip_predicted: Using applesauce in a cookie is expected to reduce spread control; using flax in a sponge is expected to reduce volume.
techniques.default_step: Match the replacer to the job: flax or chia for binding, aquafaba for foam, extra fat for richness, and starch or puree only for moisture.
